newsitem.title: CANADA: Former Bank of Canada head optimistic on economy.
newsitem.headline: Former Bank of Canada head optimistic on economy.

text.p: Former Bank of Canada Governor John Crow said on Monday that low inflation and recent declines in interest rates pointed to a year of strong growth for the Canadian economy.

"Canada does start off 1997 with some good things goings for it," Crow told Reuters in an interview. "We see the beginning of a recovery in the housing market, responding to low interest rates and the expansion in the export sector. Things look quite good I would say."
Other factors pointing to a strong year in Canada included a "very competitive" Canadian dollar, a declining deficit, a turnaround in the country's balance of payments and low inflation, Crow said.

As central bank governor from 1987 to 1994, Crow was known for his aversion to inflation. His push for price stability and willingness to raise interest rates to achieve it resulted in Canada's having one of the lowest inflation rates in the industrialized world.

Crow said it was the low inflation rate that contributed to last year's sharp declines in Canadian interest rates. Canada's central bank last year cut short-term rates 11 times, helping to bring prime lending rates in Canada to their lowest level since March 1956.

"One of my mantras was price stability. Low inflation leads to low interest rates not high ones. People say it is a high interest rate policy. If you look through it to the end result, it's a low interest rate policy," he said.

While Crow was reticent about current Bank of Canada monetary policy, he said one of the main issues facing the central bank would be the role of the 1.0 to 3.0 percent target range for inflation. The current target band is set to expire in 1998.

"You can argue that the so-called inflation targets have taken the place of the basic mandate of the Bank of Canada and that's in some ways a constructive move. It does emphasize the role of the bank vis-a-vis inflation. Whether enough has been done in that regard I think is questionable," said Crow.
While Crow would not specify what he believed should be done with the targets, he said he saw price stability as being an inflation rate of less than two percent.
